intro: The dissonances in this étude are written into the music: brief clashes and broken rhythms make the outer sections scherzando. Edward Neeman’s performance contrasts them with the slower E-major song in the middle, whose melody lies below the surrounding figuration.
question: How does the same keyboard change from clipped humour to a sustained song?

sections.label: A′ · Scherzando returns
sections.mNote: the broken rhythms return after the sustained middle song

cues.title: The clashes are composed
cues.text: The quick dissonances are part of Chopin’s writing, not mistakes by the pianist. Listen for the short, slightly displaced attacks and broken rhythms that give the outer music its scherzando character.
cues.evidence: Scherzando character and broken rhythms: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191; dissonant appoggiaturas and E-minor outer sections: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tude_Op._25,_No._5_(Chopin).

cues.title: Three publishing centres
cues.text: The Op. 25 études appeared in French, German and English editions through Schlesinger, Breitkopf & Härtel and Wessel. Printed editions could carry the same composition to different markets long before recordings circulated a pianist’s particular performance.
cues.evidence: The NIFC work record lists the French, German and English first editions and their publishers: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191

cues.title: A song below the surface
cues.text: The middle moves into E major and a slower pace. Follow the melody in the cello-like register beneath the higher figuration: the most active notes are not necessarily the tune.
cues.evidence: Middle estimated at 0:54 after a cadence and quiet 0:50 window; the score’s slower middle melody in cello register is described by https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Melody and decoration
cues.text: As the middle section grows, try keeping the low singing line distinct from the rising and falling figures around it. The two layers make different demands on attention even when played by the same pair of hands.
cues.evidence: Texture described by Tomaszewski: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191. The report’s local crest around 1:30–1:40 places the cue within the central song, not at a claimed melodic entrance.

cues.title: The second published collection
cues.text: The twelve études of Op. 25 appeared in 1837, after the Op. 10 collection. The two books give different technical tasks the variety and continuity of concert pieces, rather than presenting exercises stripped of expressive character.

cues.title: The broken rhythm returns
cues.text: After the sustained central melody, the quick scherzando writing returns. Compare the way the hands release their shorter gestures with the middle section’s longer-breathed line.
cues.evidence: Report boundary 2:28; activity and level rise around 2:30 after quieter 2:20–2:25 windows. ABA design: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedicated to Marie d’Agoult
cues.text: The Op. 25 collection is dedicated to Marie d’Agoult. This is a publishing dedication, not a programme for the individual étude: its musical contrasts do not require a biographical story.
cues.evidence: Dedication in the NIFC work record: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191

cues.title: A major ending
cues.text: The ending turns to E major rather than confirming the outer sections’ E minor. Its upward flourish and emphatic chords enlarge the scale of the close after the scherzando gestures.
cues.evidence: Coda region follows the low-level 3:05 window and renewed activity around 3:10. NIFC describes the final dramatic turn, forte chords and major-key flourish: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Short gestures give way to a low song
transitions.how: The outer music’s quick broken rhythms subside into a slower E-major middle. The melody moves into a lower, cello-like register while the other hand supplies rising and falling figuration. Tempo, mode and distribution of melody all change, giving the middle the contrasting function of a trio.
transitions.evidence: Report boundary 0:54 follows a quiet 0:50 window; formal and registral description: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191

transitions.title: The sustained song gives up its place
transitions.how: The E-major song draws back and the scherzando’s E-minor gestures return. Short attacks and broken rhythm replace the longer melodic line. Recognition rests on the outer theme’s rhythmic shape as much as on its tune: the return changes the way the piano articulates time.
transitions.evidence: Report boundary 2:28 and renewed activity at 2:30 after the central section’s decline; ABA construction: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191

transitions.title: A small scherzo gains an emphatic ending
transitions.how: The returning scherzando gives way to a more emphatic final gesture. Fuller chords and a rising flourish replace its earlier restraint, while E major displaces the surrounding E minor. The coda changes the character of the close without importing another independent theme.
transitions.evidence: Approximate junction at 3:06, following a very quiet 3:05 window and preceding renewed activity at 3:10–3:15. Closing major-key flourish: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191

facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
